record.paper_title: Open problems in theory of metric linear spaces
record.context_brief: Unbounded norms on subspaces and quotients
record.original_question: Let X be an F-space. Does X always contain an infinite-dimensional subspace that admits an equivalent unbounded F-norm, where an F-norm ||x||' is called unbounded when sup_{x in X} ||x||' = +∞? Also, does there exist a subspace M of X such that the quotient space X/M admits an unbounded F-norm?

evidence.quote: PROBLEM 2. - Does each F-space contains -an infinite dimensional subspace with unbounded norm ? Does there exist a subspace such that in the quotient space there is an unbounded norm ?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
An F-norm on a real or complex vector space X is a function ||·||: X → [0, ∞) such that: (i) ||x|| = 0 iff x = 0; (ii) ||αx|| ≤ ||x|| whenever |α| ≤ 1; (iii) lim_{α→0} ||αx|| = 0 for every x ∈ X; (iv) ||x + y|| ≤ ||x|| + ||y||. An F-space is a vector space equipped with an F-norm whose induced translation-invariant metric d(x,y) = ||x − y|| is complete. Two F-norms on X are called equivalent if they induce the same topology. An F-norm ||·||' is said to be unbounded if sup_{x ∈ X} ||x||' = +∞.

(a) Does every F-space X contain an infinite-dimensional (closed) linear subspace Y that admits an F-norm, equivalent to the restriction of the F-norm of X, which is unbounded?

(b) Does every F-space X admit a closed linear subspace M such that the quotient F-space X/M admits an equivalent unbounded F-norm?
